18.heading: CRITERIA
18.text: Provider is unable to make contact with medical control after two attempts by each of two different methods (i.e. twice via radio and twice via cell phone for a total of four attempts).

21.heading: PEARLS
21.text: Termination of resuscitation efforts is a Medical Control decision only.

21.heading: PEARLS
21.text: Resuscitation efforts and transport to the emergency department are indicated for any patient having suspected hypothermia.

21.heading: PEARLS
21.text: Consider patient's previously diagnosed medical condition.

21.heading: PEARLS
21.text: WITHHOLDING RESUSCITATION CRITERIA In accordance with Commonwealth of Virginia law, full resuscitation measures shall be undertaken for all victims of cardiopulmonary arrest except in the presence of one or more of the indications of death:

21.heading: PEARLS
21.text: The presence of one of the following: o An actual valid Virginia DDNR form o An actual valid DDNR from any State o A copy of a valid Virginia DDNR form (a digital copy is permitted) o A copy of a valid DDNR form from any State (a digital copy is permitted) o A Virginia approved DDNR ALERT bracelet or necklace o For reference, see the Code of Virginia §54.1-2987.1, § 54.1-2982

21.heading: PEARLS
21.text: Decapitation or other obvious mortal injury

21.heading: PEARLS
21.text: During mass-casualty incidents, resources must be directed toward viable patients

22.heading: PEARLS
22.text: For POST (Physician Orders for Scope of Treatment) forms, Section A qualifies as a DDNR

22.heading: PEARLS
22.text: If you have any questions regarding the orders, ask Medical Control

22.heading: PEARLS
22.text: Providers are reminded they are still not to exceed their Scope of Practice

23.heading: INDICATIONS
23.text: • Patients meeting specialty care criteria including but not limited to: o STEMI o Stroke o Trauma o Burns o Critical Pediatrics o Ventricular Assist Device (LVAD/BiVAD/VAD as directed per VAD Coordinator or Medical Control) • The air ambulance service can provide needed medical capability at the scene. • Difficult-access situations: o Wilderness rescue o Ambulance egress or access impeded at the scene by road conditions, weather, or traffic

27.heading: CRITERIA
27.text: • Any patient or surrogate decision maker refusing or declining treatment of a condition for which treatment would be otherwise indicated and/or transport via ambulance to an appropriate receiving facility

29.heading: PEARLS
29.text: For medical emergencies, issuance of an emergency custody order (ECO) for medical evaluation requires a licensed physician to petition a magistrate or special justice. Early discussion with Medical Control to provide a detailed description of the current clinical situation and concerns, assessment of decision-making capacity, and any pertinent clinical information is critical.

29.heading: PEARLS
29.text: Medical power of attorney only comes into effect when a patient lacks decision-making capacity.

29.heading: PEARLS
29.text: Attempt to obtain a copy of any documentation assigning guardianship or medical power of attorney. If unavailable, you may accept the individual’s assertion as long as you do so in good faith and do not have any evidence or knowledge that the person is misrepresenting himself/herself as a guardian or medical power of attorney.

29.heading: PEARLS
29.text: In the absence of available parents, an adult in whose care a minor has been entrusted, such as a teacher or caregiver, may act as a surrogate decision maker in the place of a parent (“in loco parentis”).

29.heading: PEARLS
29.text: A minor shall be deemed an adult for the purpose of consenting to: o Services needed to determine the presence of or to treat venereal disease of any infectious or contagious disease that the State board of Health requires to be reported o Services required in case of birth control, pregnancy or family planning o Services required in the case of outpatient care, treatment, or rehabilitation for substance abuse o Services required in the outpatient care, treatment, or rehabilitation for mental or emotional disturbance

29.heading: PEARLS
29.text: A pregnant minor shall be deemed an adult for the sole purpose of giving consent for herself and her child to surgical and medical treatment relating to the delivery of her child. Thereafter, the minor mother shall be deemed an adult for the purpose of giving consent to surgical and medical treatment for her child.

29.heading: PEARLS
29.text: Treatment and/or transport of a minor is authorized if delay may adversely affect the minor’s recovery and no authorized person is available to provide consent. If the minor is 14 years of age or older and physically capable of giving consent, such consent shall be obtained first.

45.heading: PEARLS
45.text: Transport all patients with unmanageable/uncontrolled airway or uncontrolled hemorrhage to the closest hospital emergency department.

45.heading: PEARLS
45.text: Traumatic cardiac arrest– if transporting, transport to the closest hospital emergency department.

45.heading: PEARLS
45.text: Consider transport to a pediatric center (CHKD or VCU Medical Center) for pediatric patients meeting the above trauma triage criteria.

45.heading: PEARLS
45.text: Consider transport to a burn center (Sentara Norfolk General Hospital or VCU Medical Center) for patients with burn injuries meeting the following criteria: o Partial-thickness burn of greater than 10% BSA o Electrical burns, including lightning injury o Full-thickness burns o Circumferential burns o Chemical burns

49.heading: CRITERIA
49.text: • The Universal Patient Care / Initial Patient Contact protocol applies to all patients and is the foundation for all patient care. A universal patient care protocol allows other protocols to focus on their specific goals for patient management. • While the steps listed below may occur in order, the dynamics of an emergency scene may dictate a change to the order in which they occur.

51.heading: PEARLS
51.text: Glasgow Coma Scale 1 2 3 4 5 6 Spontaneous Eye Opening Does not open Opens to Pain Opens to voice Eye opening Oriented and Incomprehensible Inappropriate Confused, Verbal Makes no sound converses sounds words disoriented normally Abnormal Flexion or Makes no Extension to pain Obeys Motor flexion to pain withdrawal to Localizes pain movement (Decerebrate) commands (Decorticate) pain Infant Age Guidelines Newborn Up to 48 hours following birth Neonates Up to 28 days following birth

55.heading: CRITERIA
55.text: • Any patient receiving invasive ventilatory support following endotracheal intubation or placement of an advanced airway including supraglottic airway devices.

55.heading: PEARLS
55.text: Adjust ventilation rate or volume to maintain EtCO2 of 35 – 45 mmHg following advanced airway placement.

55.heading: PEARLS
55.text: Closely monitor for hypotension following intubation and sedation. Positive pressure ventilation increases the risk of pneumothorax and reduced preload, both of which can result in sudden drops in mean arterial pressure.

55.heading: PEARLS
55.text: Use suction to remove blood, secretions and vomitus as needed.

55.heading: PEARLS
55.text: Use lower doses of Fentanyl for opiate naïve, frail, low weight, hypotensive, hemodynamically labile, or elderly (> 65 years) patients.

57.heading: CRITERIA
57.text: • Any patient without a palpable pulse or respiration, and with Asystole or Pulseless Electrical Activity (PEA) evidence on the cardiac monitor (check two leads), or AED advising not to shock. • Patients with a valid durable DNR, rigor mortis, lividity, decomposition, or injuries inconsistent with survival are excluded.

58.heading: PEARLS
58.text: Compressions:

58.heading: PEARLS
58.text: Push hard and fast: rate 100 – 120 bpm. Allow complete chest recoil.

58.heading: PEARLS
58.text: Minimize interruptions in chest compressions.

58.heading: PEARLS
58.text: Change compressors every 2 minutes or sooner if fatigued

58.heading: PEARLS
58.text: Give continuous compressions with advanced airway

58.heading: PEARLS
58.text: Use quantitative EtCO2 monitoring with BVM o If EtCO2 is less than 10 mmHg, improve chest compressions o If sudden increase in EtCO2 is noted (above 30-40 mmHg), check pulse and rhythm for ROSC.

58.heading: PEARLS
58.text: Airway:

58.heading: PEARLS
58.text: Use of advanced airways have not been shown to improve outcomes for children with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest. Focus on high quality BLS airway management.

58.heading: PEARLS
58.text: Studies to date have not shown a clear improvement in outcomes with SGA vs intubation – do not compromise chest compressions for intubation.

58.heading: PEARLS
58.text: Avoid excessive ventilation. Maximize preload.

58.heading: PEARLS
58.text: Use EtCO2 to confirm and monitor placement of any advanced airway.

58.heading: PEARLS
58.text: Continually monitor EtCO2 with target above 10 mmHg during CPR and 35-45 mmHg once ROSC is achieved.

58.heading: PEARLS
58.text: In post ROSC patients, if EtCO2 falls below 20 mmHg or signal is lost, immediately reassess pulses and airway.

58.heading: PEARLS
58.text: Reversible causes:

58.heading: PEARLS
58.text: Ensure IV/IO patency.

58.heading: PEARLS
58.text: Identify and treat per appropriate protocol and scope of practice: o Hypoxia o Tension pneumothorax/hemothorax o Hyperkalemia or Hypokalemia o Tamponade (Cardiac) o Hyperthermia or Hypothermia o Thrombosis (Cardiac, Pulmonary) o Hypovolemia o Toxins o Hydrogen ion (acidosis) o Trauma o Hyperglycemia or Hypoglycemia o Tablets (Overdose)

58.heading: PEARLS
58.text: Termination of Resuscitation (TOR):

58.heading: PEARLS
58.text: Refer to Death & Criteria for Withholding Resuscitation protocol.

58.heading: PEARLS
58.text: Termination of resuscitative efforts is a Medical Control decision only.

58.heading: PEARLS
58.text: Consider contacting Medical Control to request TOR if the arrest was not witnessed by EMS and after 20 minutes of continuous CPR: 1. There has been no return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) AND 2. No shocks were delivered.

59.heading: CRITERIA
59.text: • Any patient with return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) following cardiac arrest.

60.heading: PEARLS
60.text: Most patients will require at least some vasopressor support to maintain a MAP > 65 following cardiac arrest.

60.heading: PEARLS
60.text: Push dose Epinephrine may be administered as a “bridge” while establishing a drip, but does not replace a drip.

60.heading: PEARLS
60.text: Administer vasopressor through the largest, most proximal IV site available (AC or higher is preferable) or IO. Verify patency prior to initiating infusion and monitor closely for extravasation.

60.heading: PEARLS
60.text: Maintain normal ventilation rate. Continually monitor EtCO2 with target range being 35 – 45 mmHg.

60.heading: PEARLS
60.text: Identify and treat potentially reversible causes of cardiac arrest: o Hypoxia o Tension pneumothorax/hemothorax o Hyperkalemia or hypokalemia o Tamponade (Cardiac) o Hyperglycemia or hypoglycemia o Thrombosis (Cardiac/pulmonary) o Hypovolemia o Toxins o Hydrogen Ion (acidosis) o Trauma o Tablets (overdose)

61.heading: CRITERIA
61.text: • Any patient who has experienced blunt or penetrating trauma and is pulseless with apnea/agonal respirations. • Patients with obvious signs of death are excluded.

62.heading: PEARLS
62.text: Unless loss of pulses is witnessed by EMS with immediate intervention, survival following traumatic cardiac arrest with an initial rhythm of asystole is very low (<1%). Providers must weigh the risks of resuscitation and transport (injury, infectious exposure etc.) against the potential benefit prior to initiating resuscitation.

62.heading: PEARLS
62.text: When possible, assess rhythm prior to initiating CPR. If the rhythm is asystole on arrival of EMS, consider withholding resuscitation.

62.heading: PEARLS
62.text: *Unlike non-traumatic cardiac arrest, the efficacy of CPR in trauma resuscitation is unclear. Prioritize addressing immediate reversible causes of hypotension/cardiac arrest such as chest decompression, volume expansion (preferably with whole blood), and airway management. CPR is needed, however, to circulate transfused blood and any medications or fluids administered.

62.heading: PEARLS
62.text: If available, blood products should be used rather than sodium chloride for treatment of hemorrhagic shock.

62.heading: PEARLS
62.text: Assess the scene and patient closely. If the degree of sustained trauma appears disproportionately minor, consider the possibility a medical incident may have preceded or been induced by the injury. If there is suspicion for a medical event, refer to the appropriate patient care protocol.

63.heading: CRITERIA
63.text: • Any patient unresponsive, without palpable pulse or respiration, and Ventricular Fibrillation (V-Fib) or Ventricular Tachycardia (V-Tach) apparent on the cardiac monitor (check 2 leads), or AED advising to shock. • Patients with a valid durable DNR or injuries inconsistent with survival are excluded.

65.heading: PEARLS
65.text: Compressions:

65.heading: PEARLS
65.text: Push hard and fast: rate 100 – 120 bpm. Allow complete chest recoil.

65.heading: PEARLS
65.text: A common cause of refractory VF / VT is incorrect defibrillator pad placement. Ensure optimal initial placement and consider adjustment is multiple shocks are delivered without a change in rhythm.

65.heading: PEARLS
65.text: Minimize interruptions in chest compressions.

65.heading: PEARLS
65.text: Change compressors every 2 minutes or sooner if fatigued

65.heading: PEARLS
65.text: Give continuous compressions with advanced airway

65.heading: PEARLS
65.text: Use quantitative EtCO2 monitoring with BVM o If EtCO2 is less than 10 mmHg, improve chest compressions o If sudden increase in EtCO2 is noted (above 30-40 mmHg), check pulse and rhythm for ROSC.

65.heading: PEARLS
65.text: Medications:

65.heading: PEARLS
65.text: Medications should be given without interruption of CPR.

65.heading: PEARLS
65.text: Magnesium Sulfate should be considered for: Torsades de pointes, long QT, digitalis toxicity, or suspected hypomagnesemia.

65.heading: PEARLS
65.text: If there is no Epinephrine 0.1 mg/mL preloaded syringe, combine 1 mg of Epinephrine 1 mg/mL with 9 mL of 0.9% sodium chloride in a 10 mL syrine.

65.heading: PEARLS
65.text: Airway:

65.heading: PEARLS
65.text: Use of advanced airways have not been shown to improve outcomes for children with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest. Focus on high quality BLS airway management.

65.heading: PEARLS
65.text: Studies to date have not shown a clear improvement in outcomes with SGA vs intubation – do not compromise chest compressions for intubation.

65.heading: PEARLS
65.text: Avoid excessive ventilation. Maximize preload.

65.heading: PEARLS
65.text: Use EtCO2 to confirm and monitor placement of any advanced airway.

65.heading: PEARLS
65.text: Continually monitor EtCO2 with target above 10 mmHg during CPR and 35-45 mmHg once ROSC is achieved.

65.heading: PEARLS
65.text: In post ROSC patients, if EtCO2 falls below 20 mmHg or signal is lost, immediately reassess pulses and airway.

65.heading: PEARLS
65.text: Reversible causes:

65.heading: PEARLS
65.text: Identify and treat per appropriate protocol and scope of practice: o Hypoxia o Tension pneumothorax/hemothorax o Hyperkalemia or Hypokalemia o Tamponade (Cardiac) o Hyperthermia or Hypothermia o Thrombosis (Cardiac, Pulmonary) o Hypovolemia o Toxins o Hydrogen ion (acidosis) o Trauma o Hyperglycemia or Hypoglycemia o Tablets (Overdose)

67.heading: CRITERIA
67.text: Patient exposed to extreme environmental conditions with symptoms that might include, but are not limited to: • CNS depression • Cardiac dysrhythmias • Abnormal vital signs • Suspect hypothermia in: o High-risk patients: very young or old patients, immobilized patients (e.g. prolonged entrapment), alcohol use, trauma/significant burns o High-risk environment: cold, windy environments, acute immersion incident

67.heading: PEARLS
67.text: Hypothermia patients are fragile: Rough handling, IV insertion, intubation, etc. might cause VF that is refractory to defibrillation and antiarrhythmic agents- use AHA guidelines for hypothermic arrest.

67.heading: PEARLS
67.text: DO NOT place heat packs, hot water bottles, IV bags, or other heat-retaining devices directly on skin

67.heading: PEARLS
67.text: Contact Medical Control prior to use of AED

67.heading: PEARLS
67.text: If cardiac arrest occurs, start CPR. Do not delay transport waiting for ALS

67.heading: PEARLS
67.text: If the patient is alert and responsive, use active external rewarming with heat packs, warm blankets, etc

67.heading: PEARLS
67.text: Assess pulse and respiratory rate for at least 60 seconds.

67.heading: PEARLS
67.text: In Localized injuries DO NOT: o Allow patient to use the affected part o Rub the affected part o Expose the part to direct dry heat o Immerse the part in snow or hot water o Attempt to debride blisters

67.heading: PEARLS
67.text: During cardiac arrest, medications should be spaced at longer intervals

69.heading: CRITERIA
69.text: Patient exposed to extreme environmental conditions with symptoms that might include but are not limited to: • CNS depression • Cardiac dysrhythmias • Abnormal vital signs

69.heading: PEARLS
69.text: Consider cold IV fluids, if available, in heat stroke patient only. Use caution in the conscious patient

71.heading: CRITERIA
71.text: • Any patient with signs and/or symptoms of a psychiatric, medical, or traumatic emergency with agitated, aggressive, or combative behavior which poses a significant risk of harm to himself/herself or others. • For patients less than 25 kg who cannot be safely managed with de-escalation techniques (see below), contact medical control for guidance.

72.heading: PEARLS
72.text: Mild agitation = anxious, apprehensive demeanor but non-aggressive.

72.heading: PEARLS
72.text: Moderate agitation = pulling at tubes/catheters or aggressive behavior without violence.

72.heading: PEARLS
72.text: Severe agitation = overt combativeness, violence or self-harm / immediate danger to self or staff.

72.heading: PEARLS
72.text: “Persons who lack decision-making capacity are assessed and treated with implied consent. EMS practitioners must maintain the patient’s dignity to the extent possible, including use of the least restrictive method of restraint that protects the patient, the public, and emergency responders from harm. The use of appropriate de- escalation techniques should take precedence over physical restraint or pharmacologic management whenever possible.” – National Association of EMS Physicians, Clinical Care and Restraint of Agitated or Combative Patients by EMS Practitioners, October 2020.

72.heading: PEARLS
72.text: * Consider potential medical or traumatic causes of altered mental status. These include head injury, hypoxia, delirium, stroke, seizure, toxic ingestion/overdose, medication reactions, CNS infection, hyperthermia, and endocrine emergencies such as hypoglycemia and thyrotoxicosis.

72.heading: PEARLS
72.text: ** De-escalation guidelines: o Remain calm and friendly. Be aware of your emotions. o Be mindful of body language. Allow space and assume a non-threatening posture. o Position yourself between the patient and exit. o Maintain a safe distance. o Ideally, one provider should establish rapport and communicate with the patient.

75.heading: CRITERIA
75.text: • Any patient with uncontrolled or profuse external bleeding. • For general management of injured patients, refer to Trauma protocol.

76.heading: PEARLS
76.text: Hemodialysis access sites may result in life threatening hemorrhage. Direct pressure/pressure dressing should be used first; followed by tourniquet in the setting of life-threatening hemorrhage.

76.heading: PEARLS
76.text: Ensure date/time/location of placement is written on tourniquet.

76.heading: PEARLS
76.text: Do not release tourniquet once applied.

76.heading: PEARLS
76.text: If a tourniquet is placed, an alert patient may require analgesia to manage tourniquet-associated discomfort. See Pain Control protocol.

76.heading: PEARLS
76.text: If extremity wound is not accessible, a tourniquet may be placed high on the extremity. Follow manufacturer’s recommendations.

77.heading: CRITERIA
77.text: • Any patient with discomfort/pain caused by injury or illness. • Ensure the patient is not hypotensive or at significant risk of hypotension. o Infants 0 – 12 months: SBP greater than 70 mmHg o Children 1 – 10 years: SBP greater than 80 mmHg o Children and adults over 10 years: SBP greater than 100

79.heading: PEARLS
79.text: Administer Narcan (Naloxone) respiratory depression occurs. Refer to Overdose / Poisoning / Toxic Ingestions protocol.

79.heading: PEARLS
79.text: Both the Wong-Baker (FACES) chart and FLACC scale can be used to assess pain in non-verbal patients including infants and children.

79.heading: PEARLS
79.text: Even at therapeutic doses, opiates may cause respiratory/CNS depression, bradycardia and/or hypotension. Monitor vitals closely following any administration.

79.heading: PEARLS
79.text: Associated factors which may affect hemodynamics and/or respiratory sufficiency including trauma, intoxication or illness must be considered when determining whether to administer opiates for pain control and, if so, at what dose.

79.heading: PEARLS
79.text: The goal of analgesia is not to completely alleviate pain, but to reduce pain to a manageable level which allows for safe and humane treatment and transport.

79.heading: PEARLS
79.text: Consider non-pharmacologic options such as reassurance, distraction, positioning, splinting and/or cold therapy when drug therapies are either contraindicated or as an adjunct to drug therapy.

81.heading: CRITERIA
81.text: • Blunt trauma and distracting injury • Altered mental status or suspected intoxication with possible spinal injury • Neurological complaint associated with trauma (numbness or weakness present) • Trauma patients with spinal pain, tenderness, or deformity • High energy mechanism of injury with the patient unable to communicate • Any clinical suspicious of injury • Age greater than or equal to 18 years

82.heading: PEARLS
82.text: Any time the EMS provider is unsure whether spinal immobilization is appropriate or not, the EMS provider should consult with online Medical Control to determine appropriate therapy.

82.heading: PEARLS
82.text: The long spine board should be used as an extrication device and may not be required for all patients.

82.heading: PEARLS
82.text: The long spine board is beneficial for providing a firm surface to perform CPR on.

82.heading: PEARLS
82.text: Utilization of the long spine board should take into consideration the risks versus the benefits for specific patient care and should be documented on the PCR.

82.heading: PEARLS
82.text: Patients who are ambulatory at the scene of blunt trauma generally do not require spinal immobilization, however careful assessment and consideration must be evaluated.

82.heading: PEARLS
82.text: Whether or not a long spinal board is utilized, spinal precautions are still very important in patients at risk for spinal injury. Adequate spinal precautions may be achieved by placement of a C-collar (or similar device) and securing the patient firmly to the ambulance stretcher, ensuring minimal movement.

82.heading: PEARLS
82.text: Self-extrication of patients from vehicles involved in motor vehicle accidents may best be achieved with guidance by the EMS provider. This may, in some cases, lessen the amount of movement that may occur to the patient during an extrication when the patient is not entrapped.

82.heading: PEARLS
82.text: Spinal immobilization may be achieved by multiple appropriate methods. Some patients, due to size or age may not be able to be immobilized by traditional spinal immobilization procedures.

83.heading: CRITERIA
83.text: • Any patient who has experienced blunt or penetrating traumatic injury.

84.heading: PEARLS
84.text: *Shock Index = Heart Rate / Systolic Blood Pressure. Higher shock indices correlate with increased risk of post- intubation hypotension and cardiac arrest. Shock Index > 1.0 in an injured patient suggests the need for resuscitation prior to positive-pressure ventilation.

84.heading: PEARLS
84.text: Do not delay transport to establish IV lines or wait for ALS.

84.heading: PEARLS
84.text: Any patient who is cool/diaphoretic and tachycardic is considered to be in shock until proven otherwise.

84.heading: PEARLS
84.text: When possible, obtain two large bore IV access sites.

84.heading: PEARLS
84.text: Stable patients with isolated spinal injuries: handle with the utmost care. Rapid transport is not indicated.

84.heading: PEARLS
84.text: All pregnant patients who have suffered blunt trauma should be encouraged to be evaluated in an emergency department, preferably at a facility with L&D capability for patients >20 weeks gestation. Pregnant patients in the third trimester should be transported with the backboard angled to the left and slightly elevated.

84.heading: PEARLS
84.text: Vasopressors worsen hemorrhage and are generally not indicated for the management of trauma.

84.heading: PEARLS
84.text: BLS care is generally preferred in the prehospital management of major trauma. Safe and rapid transport to an appropriate hospital is indicated with ideal scene-time less than 10 minutes. Consider the benefit/risk of performing ALS interventions during transport.

84.heading: PEARLS
84.text: Consider HEMS if the patient meets one or more of the applicable trauma triage criteria. HEMS is best utilized when the expected level of care exceeds available capabilities AND the patient can be transported by air in a similar or shorter time than the patient could be transported by ground. Be sure to consider the additional time required for rendezvous and patient transfer when considering HEMS.

87.heading: CRITERIA
87.text: • Any patient with radiation, chemical, or thermal burns.

88.heading: PEARLS
88.text: Assess for airway / inhalation injury. Consider early definitive airway management for patients with respiratory distress, hoarse voice or stridor, carbonaceous sputum and/or facial burns. Prompt assessment by a qualified RSI paramedic, when available, is preferred.

88.heading: PEARLS
88.text: Immediate (pre-hospital) hypotension solely due to burns < 20% TBSA is unlikely. Assess patients with hypotension/AMS in the setting of limited burns for concomitant trauma or other medical conditions (e.g. cardiac emergency or cyanide poisoning).

88.heading: PEARLS
88.text: Only if necessary (i.e. no other accessible site), obtain IV/IO access through a burned area.

88.heading: PEARLS
88.text: Utilize reverse triage (i.e. treat pulseless/apneic patients first) in the case of lightning strike with multiple patients. Cardiac arrest is likely to be due to airway obstruction or shockable arrhythmia (VF/VT).

88.heading: PEARLS
88.text: Treat road-rash as a burn injury. Assess closely for concomitant blunt trauma.

88.heading: PEARLS
88.text: Hydrofluoric Acid (HF) – binds and rapidly reduces serum calcium leading to circulatory collapse. Treat hypotension with 1 g Calcium Chloride IV/IO over 3 minutes. Repeat in 5 minutes as needed.

88.heading: PEARLS
88.text: Addressing hemodynamic instability, airway compromise and/or major traumatic injuries takes priority over direct transport to a burn center. Do not bypass a trauma center to transport to a burn center if the patient is unstable.

91.heading: CRITERIA
91.text: • Any patient with a trapped/crushed extremity or torso for more than 30 minutes. • Any patient who has experienced a crush injury or prolonged entrapment and is in cardiac arrest or has one or more of the following ECG change suggestive of hyperkalemia: o Peaked T waves o Ectopic beats o Prolonged PR segment (>200 ms) o Arrhythmia (e.g. ventricular o Flattening or loss of P waves tachycardia) o Wide QRS complex

92.heading: PEARLS
92.text: Crush syndrome involves the release of toxins, particularly large amounts of potassium, from skeletal muscle cells following blunt trauma and prolonged soft tissue ischemia. Prehospital treatment is focused on preventing or treating life-threatening arrhythmia due to hyperkalemia. Crush injuries are not limited to heavy weights applied to extremities for a prolonged time and can occur in a variety of situations such are after prolonged suspension in a harness or following a prolonged time laying on a hard surface.

92.heading: PEARLS
92.text: Sodium bicarbonate and Calcium Chloride are preferably given via separate IV lines to avoid precipitation into Calcium Carbonate. If separate IV sites cannot be obtained, flush with at least 20 mL saline between drugs.

92.heading: PEARLS
92.text: Continuous albuterol is given to treat suspected hyperkalemia in the setting of persistent ECG changes.

92.heading: PEARLS
92.text: IV fluids may worsen bleeding. Use clinical judgement when administering fluids to patients with crush injuries, balancing risk of hemorrhage vs benefit in treating crush syndrome.

92.heading: PEARLS
92.text: Widened QRS: Adult > 120 ms, Pediatric > 90 ms

93.heading: CRITERIA
93.text: • Any patient who has suffered an acute submersion / non-fatal drowning event. • Any patient with one or more of the following symptoms of decompression injury after breathing compressed air at depth: o Altered mental status o Chest pain o Seizures o Headache o Vision changes o Focal neurologic signs o Respiratory distress o Ataxia o Hemoptysis o Pain in joints / extremities

94.heading: PEARLS
94.text: Caution: rewarming the extremities before the trunk may lead to vasodilation, resulting in a drop in blood pressure.

94.heading: PEARLS
94.text: Trauma very commonly occurs along with submersion / drowning. Maintain a high suspicion for blunt trauma, particularly involving the head and spine.

94.heading: PEARLS
94.text: Patients in cardiac arrest following cold-water submersion have been reported to survive neurologically intact even following prolonged resuscitation. Contact Medical Control for guidance regarding continued on-scene resuscitation vs transport to the closest emergency department.

94.heading: PEARLS
94.text: Handle patients with hypothermia gently – rough handling may precipitate arrythmias including lethal VF.

94.heading: PEARLS
94.text: Pulmonary edema may develop hours after a submersion event. Transport of all patients who have experienced nonfatal drowning for assessment and observation is encouraged.

94.heading: PEARLS
94.text: * Rapid ascent after breathing compressed air at depth may lead to barotrauma including injury to the lungs (pneumothorax). Evaluate and treat as you would any other trauma patient, beginning with a complete head- to-toe assessment.

94.heading: PEARLS
94.text: * Rapid ascent may also lead to the formation of gas bubbles in the soft tissues, causing pain (i.e. “the bends”). These bubbles may also form within the vasculature (arterial gas emboli) which can present as a variety of emergencies including seizure, stroke, MI or PE. Initial treatment is centered on identification, stabilization, and transport to an appropriate facility.

96.heading: CRITERIA
96.text: Any patient exhibiting signs of symptoms of electrical contact injury or who may have been struck by lightning.

97.heading: PEARLS
97.text: Assess for airway / inhalation injury. Consider early definitive airway management for patients with respiratory distress, hoarse voice or stridor, carbonaceous sputum and/or facial burns. Prompt assessment by a qualified RSI paramedic, when available, is preferred.

97.heading: PEARLS
97.text: Immediate (pre-hospital) hypotension solely due to burns < 20% TBSA is unlikely. Assess patients with hypotension/AMS in the setting of limited burns for concomitant trauma or other medical conditions (e.g. cardiac emergency or cyanide poisoning).

97.heading: PEARLS
97.text: Only if necessary (i.e. no other accessible site), obtain IV/IO access through a burned area.

97.heading: PEARLS
97.text: Utilize reverse triage (i.e. treat pulseless/apneic patients first) in the case of lightning strike with multiple patients. Cardiac arrest is likely to be due to airway obstruction or shockable arrhythmia (VF/VT).

97.heading: PEARLS
97.text: Addressing hemodynamic instability, airway compromise and/or major traumatic injuries takes priority over direct transport to a burn center. Do not bypass a trauma center to transport to a burn center if the patient is unstable.

99.heading: CRITERIA
99.text: • Any patient with signs or symptoms of an acute allergic reaction (mild - moderate). • Any patient with signs or symptoms of an anaphylactic reaction (severe). o Two or more of the following that occur rapidly after exposure to a likely allergen: § Involvement of the skin or mucosal tissue § Respiratory distress § Hypotension of syncope § Persistent gastrointestinal symptoms (abdominal cramps, diarrhea, vomiting) o OR hypotension after exposure to a known allergen for the patient.

101.heading: PEARLS
101.text: Remove, decontaminate, or separate the patient from the allergic trigger whenever possible.

101.heading: PEARLS
101.text: If the patient is experiencing anaphylaxis with hemodynamic instability or respiratory distress, administer IM epinephrine before any other medications.

101.heading: PEARLS
101.text: EMTs may administer intramuscular epinephrine for anaphylaxis via color-coded or clearly marked syringe only.

101.heading: PEARLS
101.text: Monitor patients closely following the administration of Epinephrine, particularly patients with significant cardiopulmonary comorbidities. Obtain an ECG immediately for any patient who develops chest discomfort or other signs of cardiac ischemia following the administration of IM Epinephrine or during an Epinephrine infusion.

101.heading: PEARLS
101.text: Administer Epinephrine via infusion through the largest, most proximal IV access site that can be obtained, preferably antecubital fossa. Monitor closely for signs of extravasation including changes in skin color, pain, swelling, numbness, or tingling. Stop the infusion immediately if extravasation is suspected and resume, if needed, on the contralateral site.

101.heading: PEARLS
101.text: Close monitoring during fluid administration should include frequent reassessment of respiratory effort, lung sounds and edema.

103.heading: CRITERIA
103.text: Any patient with a sustained ventricular rate less than 60 beats per minute AND one or more of the following signs or symptoms despite adequate oxygenation and ventilation (ie UNSTABLE Bradycardia): • Hypotension (age based) • Pulmonary Edema • Signs of shock • Dyspnea • Altered mental status • Chest pain Patients with asymptomatic/STABLE bradycardia are excluded. Monitor closely for any change in status. Note: For neonates (less than 28 days of age), refer to Neonatal Resuscitation protocol.

104.heading: PEARLS
104.text: Close monitoring during fluid administration including frequent reassessment of respiratory effort, lung sounds, and edema.

104.heading: PEARLS
104.text: Do not delay pacing to obtain IV/IO access if the patient is hemodynamically unstable.

104.heading: PEARLS
104.text: Refer to manufacturer recommendations for device specific optimal pad placement.

104.heading: PEARLS
104.text: Administer vasopressors through the largest, most proximal IV site available (AC or higher preferable) or IO. Verify patency prior to initiating infusion and monitor closely for extravasation.

107.heading: CRITERIA
107.text: • Any patient reporting chest pain or discomfort • Any patient reporting symptoms which are unexplained and consistent with an atypical presentation of cardiac ischemia, such as: o Abdominal pain o Back pain o Nausea / vomiting o Neck or jaw pain / discomfort o Syncope o Arm pain / discomfort o Dyspnea

108.heading: PEARLS
108.text: Intermediate and Paramedic providers may interpret a 12-Lead ECG as STEMI if diagnostic criteria is met: o Symptoms consistent with an acute coronary syndrome or myocardial ischemia AND o ≥ 1 mm ST segment elevation in two or more contiguous leads

108.heading: PEARLS
108.text: *Contact the receiving facility via COR and provide notification of a “Pre-Hospital STEMI Alert” as well as the patient’s name and date of birth to facilitate rapid registration. Do not provide patient identifiers over the HEAR.

108.heading: PEARLS
108.text: If transport to a PCI capable hospital will not be possible within 30 minutes, consider HEMS.

108.heading: PEARLS
108.text: With prompt response, initial ECGs often do not show ischemia. When there is high suspicion for cardiac ischemia, obtain serial ECGs to assess symptoms with recent onset (< 1 hour).

108.heading: PEARLS
108.text: Do not administer Nitroglycerine (Nitrostat) to patients who have taken any long-acting nitrate-based medications within the past 48 hours. These include: Sildenafil (Viagra / Revatio), Vardenafil (Levitra) and Tadalafil (Cialis). Record 12-Lead ECG prior to nitroglycerine administration.

108.heading: PEARLS
108.text: Any unstable patient not expected to survive transport to a PCI capable hospital should be transported immediately to the nearest Emergency Department.

109.heading: CRITERIA
109.text: • Any patient with systolic blood pressure greater than 240 mmHg and/or diastolic greater than 120 mmHg. • Any patient with chronic essential hypertension and sudden, unexplained, significant increase in blood pressure.

109.heading: PEARLS
109.text: Generally, prehospital treatment of hypertension is unnecessary. Monitor for deterioration in patient condition.

109.heading: PEARLS
109.text: Patients with extremely high blood pressure may experience epistaxis (nose bleeding). If present, manage with direct pressure with the patient leaning forward.

111.heading: CRITERIA
111.text: • Any patient with symptomatic hyperglycemia (blood glucose greater than 300 mg/dL) • Any infant, child, or adult with symptomatic hypoglycemia (blood glucose less than 60 mg/dL) • Any newborn (less than 72 hours) with symptomatic hypoglycemia (blood glucose less than 40 mg/dL)

112.heading: PEARLS
112.text: Blood glucose must be assessed for any patient with altered mental status.

112.heading: PEARLS
112.text: *Response to Glucagon requires adequate stores of glycogen in the liver. Patients with liver disease, malnourishment, and some newborns/children with congenital metabolic disease may not adequately respond. If IV access cannot be obtained and there is no response to Glucagon within 5-10 minutes (or if emergent therapy is required), obtain IO access and administer Dextrose as above.

112.heading: PEARLS
112.text: Asymptomatic hyperglycemia does not require prehospital intervention. Use caution when administering IV fluids to patients with congestive heart failure, ESRD or pulmonary edema.

112.heading: PEARLS
112.text: The risk of recurrent hypoglycemia following appropriate treatment is higher in the following situations: o No clear explanation for hypoglycemia. o Nausea or vomiting that prevents adequate PO intake. o Signs/symptoms of acute illness such as infection or ACS. o Use of long-acting oral anti-hyperglycemic medications such as Sulfonylureas and SGLT2 inhibitors. o The patient is unaware of symptoms when hypoglycemic or the patient will be left alone. o Persistent vital sign abnormalities or altered mental status.

113.heading: CRITERIA
113.text: • Under 1 year of age: SBP less than 70 mmHg or MAP less than 55 mmHg • Over 1 year of age: SBP less than 90 mmHg or MAP less than 65 mmHg • No evidence of acute traumatic injury (Refer to Trauma protocol for patients with injuries) • Signs and/or symptoms of inadequate perfusion, such as: o Altered mental status o Syncope o Diaphoresis o Dyspnea o Chest pain or discomfort o Pulmonary edema

114.heading: PEARLS
114.text: This protocol is not intended for the management of patients with hypotension due to major trauma.

114.heading: PEARLS
114.text: * There are many potential causes of hypotension. Generally, the causes fall into one of four categories: cardiogenic, distributive, hypovolemic or obstructive. Alternatively, hypotension can be rapidly assessed as a: o Pump problem: Cardiac issues such as dysrhythmia, ischemia, or tamponade o Tank problem: Hypovolemia (intravascular) due to hemorrhage, vomiting, diarrhea, dehydration, sepsis or anaphylaxis o Pipe problem: Large vessel injury or obstruction such as aortic dissection or pulmonary embolism

114.heading: PEARLS
114.text: Hypotension is a late sign of shock in pediatric patients. Children with tachycardia should be assessed closely for signs of compensated shock and providers must maintain a high index of suspicion that they may progress into decompensated shock with little warning.

114.heading: PEARLS
114.text: When administering fluids to an infant or child, use a three-way stopcock and syringe to pull/push the desired volume.

114.heading: PEARLS
114.text: ** Use caution when administering IV fluids to patients with known or suspect congestive heart failure or decreased ejection fraction. Large volumes of rapidly administered fluids may lead to pulmonary edema and respiratory distress. Administer smaller boluses (250 mL then reassess) and consider early administration of vasopressors to patients unlikely to tolerate large volumes of IV fluids.

114.heading: PEARLS
114.text: Administer vasopressors through the largest, most proximal IV site available (AC or higher preferable) or IO. Verify patency prior to initiating infusion and monitor closely for signs of extravasation.

114.heading: PEARLS
114.text: Use caution when considering positive pressure ventilation for patients with hypotension, particularly due to intravascular hypovolemia (reduced pre-load). Intubation and positive pressure ventilation may lead to a sudden drop in blood pressure or circulatory collapse / cardiac arrest.

117.heading: CRITERIA
117.text: Any patient with persistent nausea or vomiting.

117.heading: PEARLS
117.text: Caution: Administer IV Ondansetron (Zofran) via slow push – at least 30 seconds, but preferably 2 minutes.

117.heading: PEARLS
117.text: Caution: Ondansetron is safe and effective at low doses but known to prolong the cardiac QT interval, increasing the risk of potentially lethal arrhythmia in patients taking other drugs which prolong the QT interval (e.g. Amiodarone, Haloperidol) and patients with pre-existing prolonged-QTc (≥ 500 ms). Assess and consider risk prior to administration.

117.heading: PEARLS
117.text: Anti-emetic medications are often more effective when given prophylactically or for nausea prior to vomiting.

117.heading: PEARLS
117.text: Maximum total dose of Ondansetron is 8 mg (Adult) or 0.3 mg/kg (Pediatric).

119.heading: CRITERIA
119.text: • Any patient with signs of symptoms of drug / medication overdose or report of toxic ingestion • For chemical / biological / radiological exposures, refer to CBRNE protocols.

121.heading: PEARLS
121.text: Contact the Poison Control Center at 1-800-222-1222 with any questions. Note: Although Poison Control can provide invaluable expert guidance, it is not online medical control. If recommendations fall outside of protocols, contact medical control for guidance.

121.heading: PEARLS
121.text: Ensure the patient is decontaminated and appropriate PPE is worn if there is any concern for dermal exposure (particularly organophosphates).

121.heading: PEARLS
121.text: Even small amounts of some drugs / medications can lead to permanent disability or death in small children. Some or all of the effects may be delayed. Maintain a low threshold to transport even well-appearing children following possible toxic ingestions and consider contacting Poison Control and/or Medical Control for guidance.

121.heading: PEARLS
121.text: Hydroxocobalamin (Cyanokit) is not provided as part of the PEMS regional drug box exchange program. Availability may vary between agencies. Dosing guidelines are provided here for reference only – refer to agency specific protocols prior to administration, if applicable.

123.heading: CRITERIA
123.text: • Any patient who exhibits signs or symptoms of respiratory distress including abnormal respiratory rate or effort, increased work of breathing, abnormal breath sounds, cyanosis, or complains of dyspnea, shortness of breath or difficulty breathing. • For respiratory distress due to an allergic reaction, refer to the Allergic Reaction / Anaphylaxis protocol.

125.heading: PEARLS
125.text: Appropriate treatment of patients experiencing respiratory distress relies on careful consideration of the underlying cause. During the initial evaluation, first assess for conditions requiring immediate action such as airway obstruction, respiratory failure requiring ventilatory support, cardiac ischemia, or tension pneumothorax/hemothorax. Refer to the condition specific protocols, as necessary.

125.heading: PEARLS
125.text: Use all available data to make an informed decision as to the most likely cause of the patient’s respiratory distress, including known recent and chronic medical history, medications and physical exam via lung assessment, presence or absence of pulmonary/peripheral edema, JVD, productive cough etc.

125.heading: PEARLS
125.text: Use caution when administering epinephrine to patients with suspected asthma/COPD/reactive airway disease who ALSO have a history or signs of congestive heart failure. Contact medical control immediately for guidance if there is any doubt as to whether epinephrine is indicated.

125.heading: PEARLS
125.text: Early use of non-invasive positive pressure ventilation (CPAP) to support work of breathing has been shown to reduce the need for intubation and improve outcomes. Positive pressure ventilation does not replace the need for treatment of the underlying cause of respiratory distress. Close monitoring for the development of hypotension and/or pneumothorax is required.

125.heading: PEARLS
125.text: In severe cases of asthma/COPD/reactive airway disease, wheezing may be slight or absent if air movement is minimal. As bronchodilator therapy takes effect and air movement increases, wheezing may paradoxically worsen before improving. In all cases, judge the effectiveness of therapy and escalate / de-escalate based on the patient’s comfort, work of breathing and vital signs.

125.heading: PEARLS
125.text: Prior to administering nitroglycerin to any patient: obtain IV access, ensure blood pressure is acceptable (SBP ≥ 100 mmHg and MAP ≥ 65), and assess for the recent use of PDE inhibitors (eg. Sildenafil, Vardenafil, Tadalafil). Note: these medications are routinely prescribed to both men and women for a variety of conditions.

127.heading: CRITERIA
127.text: • Any patient with witnessed or reported seizure-like activity • If the patient is pregnant at greater than 20 weeks gestation or up to 8 weeks post-partum AND has no known history of seizures or epilepsy, refer to Eclampsia protocol.

127.heading: PEARLS
127.text: Seizures have a multitude of causes including epilepsy, hypoglycemia, trauma, stroke, infection and a variety of chemical overdose and withdrawal conditions.

127.heading: PEARLS
127.text: Status epilepticus (two or more seizures without a return to baseline, or a single seizure lasting > 5 minutes) is an emergency requiring rapid treatment. Patients experiencing seizures refractory to benzodiazepine therapy may require airway management. Immediate transport to the closest Emergency Department is warranted.

127.heading: PEARLS
127.text: Pediatric febrile seizures are common, but transport to an emergency department for close monitoring and further evaluation is recommended.

127.heading: PEARLS
127.text: Caution: Both seizures and benzodiazepines may lead to significant respiratory depression. Monitor airway and breathing closely. Refer to Airway Management and Ventilatory Support for treatment guidelines.

129.heading: CRITERIA
129.text: • Suspected infection with measure temperature greater than 38°C / 100.4°F or less than 36°C / 96.8°F • AND two or more of the following criteria < 1 month 1 mo – 1 yr 2 – 5 years 6 – 12 years 13 years + Mentation Lethargic, Altered Mental Status High Risk Immunocompromised, Malignancy, Indwelling catheters/tech, Sickle Cell Disease Bradycardia < 100 < 90 N/A Systolic BP Less than 70 mmHg Less than 90 mmHg MAP Less than 55 mmHg Less than 65 mmHg Respiratory Rate > 60 > 30 Capillary Refill Greater than 3 seconds EtCO2 Less than 25 mmHg

130.heading: PEARLS
130.text: *Use caution when administering IV fluids to patients with known or suspect congestive heart failure or decreased ejection fraction. Septic patients may be at higher risk of developing pulmonary edema and acute respiratory distress. Monitor closely for fluid overload. Large volumes of rapidly administered fluids may lead to pulmonary edema and respiratory distress. Administer smaller boluses (eg 250 mL then reassess) and consider early administration of vasopressors to patients unlikely to tolerate large volumes of IV fluids. If risk vs benefit of either therapy is in doubt or unclear, contact medical control for guidance.

130.heading: PEARLS
130.text: High risk patients for sepsis and septic shock include: Age < 56 days (8 weeks), presence of an indwelling catheter, malignancy, asplenia/sickle cell disease, use of immunosuppressant medications and any other immunocompromised condition.

130.heading: PEARLS
130.text: Administer vasopressor through the largest, most proximal IV site available (AC or higher preferable) or IO. Verify patency prior to initiating infusion and monitor closely for signs of extravasation such as pain, skin pallor, absent distal pulses, and/or swelling at the infusion site.

130.heading: PEARLS
130.text: Prehospital sepsis screening and notification have been shown to reduce time to treatment in Emergency Departments and improve mortality.

130.heading: PEARLS
130.text: Refer to Hypotension / Shock protocol for vasopressor drip reference charts.

131.heading: CRITERIA
131.text: • Any patient presenting with new neurologic symptoms indicative of stroke (BEFAST) including: o Altered mental status o Abnormal or slurred speech o Facial droop o Unilateral weakness o Balance of gait instability o Vision changes. • BEFAST = Balance, Eyes, Face, Arms, Speech, Time

132.heading: PEARLS
132.text: It is critical to determine, whenever possible, the time of onset of any acute neurologic symptoms. These include headache, weakness, slurred speech, dizziness, altered mental status or any other symptoms that may be consistent with acute stroke.

132.heading: PEARLS
132.text: Bring any medications or medication list, if available, with the patient.

132.heading: PEARLS
132.text: To expedite assessment in the ED, be prepared to answer questions regarding anticoagulant use, recent surgeries or trauma, bleeding disorders, or prior stroke.

132.heading: PEARLS
132.text: To facilitate rapid imaging, an 18g IV in the right antecubital (AC) site is preferred.

132.heading: PEARLS
132.text: Approximately 85% of patients diagnosed with a large vessel occlusion have a RACE score ≥ 5. Approximately 69% of patients with a RACE score ≥ 5 will be diagnosed with an LVO. For these patients, endovascular therapy (available only at comprehensive/thrombectomy capable stoke centers) has been shown to lead to better long- term outcomes.

132.heading: PEARLS
132.text: Any patient with an immediate life-threat (e.g. uncontrolled airway, cardiac arrest) that cannot be addressed during transport should be transported to the nearest emergency department.

132.heading: PEARLS
132.text: Call COR at the receiving facility to inform of the patient’s name and date of birth for rapid registration.

135.heading: CRITERIA
135.text: • Any patient with sustained supraventricular tachycardia (SVT). • SVT: Narrow complex (Adult < 120 ms, Ped < 90 ms), rate usually > 150 bpm, no P waves • Patients with chest pain, dyspnea, altered mental status, pulmonary edema, or other signs/symptoms of shock should be considered unstable. • For wide complex tachycardias, refer to Ventricular Tachycardia with a Pulse.

136.heading: PEARLS
136.text: Unstable vs stable: Unstable patients are those with signs/symptoms consistent with poor or inadequate perfusion (chest pain, AMS, hypotension, diaphoresis, respiratory distress etc). Compensated vs decompensated tachycardia is another way of describing this difference. Stable/compensated patients may be symptomatic (palpitations or mild shortness of breath with exertion, for example) but are not in extremis.

136.heading: PEARLS
136.text: There are many potential causes for tachyarrhythmias including heart disease, fever, sepsis, trauma, pain, hypoxia, hypovolemia, hypoglycemia, toxic ingestion, myocardial infarction, pulmonary embolism, electrolyte abnormalities and many others. Prehospital therapy is based on early identification and treatment of unstable arrythmias and those at risk of rapid deterioration as well as the inciting factor.

136.heading: PEARLS
136.text: Many patients who experience tachyarrhythmias have concurrent congestive heart failure or decreased ejection fraction. Exercise caution when providing IV fluids – give only enough to improve perfusion and monitor for signs of pulmonary edema.

136.heading: PEARLS
136.text: In rare cases, electrical cardioversion to sinus rhythm can result in embolization of small blood clots from the heart, leading to stroke. Following emergent cardioversion, monitor closely for changes in mental status or physical exam and reassess destination choice as appropriate.

136.heading: PEARLS
136.text: Dosing of electrical therapy described above serves as a guideline only. Confirm agency dosing for cardioversion and defibrillation with device specific manufacturers recommendations.

136.heading: PEARLS
136.text: Ensure the device is set to SYNC prior to any attempted cardioversion of a patient with a palpable pulse. Unsynchronized cardioversion/defibrillation may lead to ventricular fibrillation and cardiac arrest.

137.heading: CRITERIA
137.text: • Any patient with sustained ventricular tachycardia with a palpable pulse. • Ventricular tachycardia: Wide complex (Adult > 120 ms, Ped > 90 ms), no P waves, usual rate > 150 bpm • Patients with chest pain, dyspnea, altered mental status, pulmonary edema, or other signs/symptoms of shock should be considered unstable.

138.heading: PEARLS
138.text: Unstable vs stable: Unstable patients are those with signs/symptoms consistent with poor or inadequate perfusion (chest pain, AMS, hypotension, diaphoresis, respiratory distress etc). Compensated vs decompensated tachycardia is another way of describing this difference. Stable/compensated patients may be symptomatic (palpitations or mild shortness of breath with exertion, for example) but are not in extremis.

138.heading: PEARLS
138.text: There are many potential causes for tachyarrhythmias including heart disease, fever, sepsis, trauma, pain, hypoxia, hypovolemia, hypoglycemia, toxic ingestion, myocardial infarction, pulmonary embolism, electrolyte abnormalities and many others. Prehospital therapy is based on early identification and treatment of unstable arrythmias and those at risk of rapid deterioration as well as the inciting factor.

138.heading: PEARLS
138.text: Many patients who experience tachyarrhythmias have concurrent congestive heart failure or decreased ejection fraction. Exercise caution when providing IV fluids – give only enough to improve perfusion and monitor for signs of pulmonary edema.

138.heading: PEARLS
138.text: In rare cases, electrical cardioversion to sinus rhythm can result in embolization of small blood clots from the heart, leading to stroke. Following emergent cardioversion, monitor closely for changes in mental status or physical exam and reassess destination choice as appropriate.

138.heading: PEARLS
138.text: Dosing of electrical therapy described above serves as a guideline only. Confirm agency dosing for cardioversion and defibrillation with device specific manufacturers recommendations.

138.heading: PEARLS
138.text: Ensure the device is set to SYNC prior to any attempted cardioversion of a patient with a palpable pulse. Unsynchronized cardioversion/defibrillation may lead to ventricular fibrillation and cardiac arrest.

138.heading: PEARLS
138.text: If the rhythm is polymorphic ventricular tachycardia, synchronization may not be possible. This is the only time a patient with a palpable pulse is treated with unsynchronized defibrillation.

141.heading: CRITERIA
141.text: • Any patient with known or suspected pregnancy and symptoms of term or pre-term labor (contractions, loss of fluid, vaginal bleeding and/or urge to push)

142.heading: PEARLS
142.text: Patients who are known or suspected to be pregnant and are experiencing profuse vaginal bleeding should be transported to a facility with obstetric capability if patient condition and geographic constraints allow. o Conditions such as uterine rupture and placental abruption are rare but cannot be managed effectively in the field and will most likely present with severe abdominal pain and symptoms consistent with hemorrhagic shock.

142.heading: PEARLS
142.text: Gestational age can be approximated by the palpable height of the uterine fundus, with 20 weeks being roughly the height of the umbilicus. Resuscitation should be attempted for any fetus born after 22 weeks gestational age. If unsure of gestational age or viability, initiate resuscitative efforts by following the Neonatal Resuscitation protocol and contact medical control for guidance.

142.heading: PEARLS
142.text: Rupture of membranes (loss of fluid) prior to 37 weeks gestation is considered premature. These patients are at an increased risk of umbilical cord prolapse and need for resuscitation of the neonate.

142.heading: PEARLS
142.text: Hypotension not associated with blood loss should be addressed with IV fluids and, if possible, relieving weight on the IVC by placing the patient in a left lateral recumbent position.

142.heading: PEARLS
142.text: Consider requesting an additional transport unit to the scene to care for the neonate if delivery is imminent.

142.heading: PEARLS
142.text: No NOT apply pressure to the uterine fundus. Suprapubic pressure is used to guide the fetus under the pubic symphysis.

142.heading: PEARLS
142.text: Normal newborn SpO2 is 60-70% in the first minute of life, 80-85% at five minutes, and 85-95% at ten minutes.

147.heading: CRITERIA
147.text: • Pre-eclampsia with severe features: Any pregnant (or recently pregnant) patient over 20 weeks gestational age presenting with one or more of the following: o Systolic blood pressure greater than 160 mmHg or diastolic blood pressure greater than 110 mmHg o Severe and/or persistent headache o Right upper quadrant or epigastric abdominal pain o New onset of visual disturbance o Pulmonary edema • Eclampsia: Any pregnant or recently pregnant patient over 20 weeks gestational age experiencing seizures.

147.heading: PEARLS
147.text: Pre-Eclampsia and Eclampsia can occur up to 8 weeks AFTER delivery of the baby.

147.heading: PEARLS
147.text: The primary goal of therapy is to prevent or limit seizures, and rapid intervention is warranted. If administration of Magnesium will be delayed due to lack of IV/IO access or need for reconstitution, consider early IM administration of midazolam followed by Magnesium infusion as soon as feasible.

147.heading: PEARLS
147.text: For the patient who presents with pre-eclampsia and deteriorates to eclampsia (seizes), the total maximum dose is 4g Magnesium Sulfate.

147.heading: PEARLS
147.text: Provide early notification to the hospital as non-ED care teams such as OBGYN and anesthesia may need to be mobilized.

147.heading: PEARLS
147.text: Caution: Administration of Magnesium and Benzodiazepines may lead to respiratory/CNS depression.

147.heading: PEARLS
147.text: Caution: rapid administration of Magnesium may cause vasodilation and hypotension – monitor vitals at least every 5 minutes during infusion and stop infusion immediately if hypotension develops.

149.heading: CRITERIA
149.text: Uterine Rupture - Severe vaginal bleeding in the second half of pregnancy.

149.heading: PEARLS
149.text: Should be suspected in the pregnant trauma patient who has lost the palpable uterine contour, has easily palpated fetal parts, and who has severe abdominal pain. ABRUPTIO PLACENTA

149.heading: CRITERIA
149.text: Premature separation of the placenta from the uterine wall after the 20th week of gestation and prior to birth. EMR Follow General – Universal Patient Care/Initial Patient Contact protocol. EMR EMR Support life threatening problems associated with airway, breathing and circulation. EMR EMR Administer oxygen as needed per patient assessment. EMR EMR If patient exhibits signs of shock, see Medical – Hypotension/Shock (Non-trauma). EMR EMR Place patient in left lateral recumbent position and transport immediately. EMR Establish IV access and administer 20 mL/kg 0.9% Normal Saline bolus up to a A total of 1,000 mL; continuously reassess need for further fluid administration. A

149.heading: PEARLS
149.text: Patients younger than 20 and greater than 35 years of age are at greater risk for placental abruption.

153.heading: CRITERIA
153.text: • Any patient with likely exposure to a choking agent / airway irritant and one or more of the following symptoms: o Difficulty breathing / respiratory distress o Throat pain / burning o Wheezing o Laryngospasm o Non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema • For respiratory distress due to nerve agents / organophosphates, refer to Nerve Agents protocol.

154.heading: PEARLS
154.text: The decision to enter a contaminated area to rescue and/or provide patient care rests with the incident commander and organizational policy.

154.heading: PEARLS
154.text: Victims that have been decontaminated and/or confirmed “clean” are safe for treatment and transportation to a health care facility. Examples of common choking agents:

154.heading: PEARLS
154.text: Hydrofluoric Acid Concept of treatment protocol:

154.heading: PEARLS
154.text: Reduce the dose o Rescue from environment o Decontamination

154.heading: PEARLS
154.text: Support cardiovascular system / perfusion Contact the Poison Control Center at 1-800-222-1222 with any questions. Note: Although Poison Control can provide invaluable expert guidance, it is not online medical control. If recommendations fall outside of protocols, contact medical control for guidance.

155.heading: CRITERIA
155.text: • Any patient with likely exposure to a biological / infectious agent and one or more of the following otherwise unexplained symptoms: o Fever o Shortness of breath o Gastrointestinal symptoms o Rash • Any patient with close contact with a person with a confirmed or suspected diagnosis of an infectious biological agent such as: o Anthrax o Plague o Smallpox o Hemorrhagic Fever (e.g. Ebola, Marburg)

155.heading: PEARLS
155.text: Responders should wear a minimum of N-95 respirators with airborne and contact PPE (Level C) when responding to non-specific flu-like symptoms in the setting of a suspected biological incident. Higher levels of PPE may be warranted depending on the suspected biological / infectious agent.

155.heading: PEARLS
155.text: A surgical mask may be placed on the patient with suspected infection, under a non-rebreather mask if necessary.

155.heading: PEARLS
155.text: Contact the local health department to determine whether antibiotic prophylaxis is required for first responders and/or close contacts.

157.heading: CRITERIA
157.text: • Any patient with suspected exposure to a blistering agent (including asymptomatic exposure) • Any patient with possible exposure to a blistering agent and signs or symptoms of skin or mucous membrane irritation and/or respiratory distress.

157.heading: PEARLS
157.text: Blistering agents pose a significant risk of exposure to first responders. They are difficult to remove during decontamination and often do not provide immediate signs of contamination. Ensure appropriate PPE is worn during patient contact and maintain a low threshold for gross decontamination.

157.heading: PEARLS
157.text: Skin penetration is rapid. Mustard agents cause both localized cellular damage and systemic damage. A large liquid or vapor exposure causes immune system failure and pulmonary damage. Sepsis and pulmonary damage the major causes of death.

157.heading: PEARLS
157.text: Blister agents are powerful skin and mucous membrane irritants and vesicants, produce corrosion and necrosis of the skin, eyes, and respiratory tract. While the chemical reaction with biological tissue occurs rapidly, symptoms are typically delayed by several hours. Systemic poisoning occurs more easily in warm climates.

157.heading: PEARLS
157.text: DERMAL exposure: Signs and symptoms typically occurs within 2 – 24 hours of exposure. Itching and erythema occur 2 to 3 hours after dermal exposure to gas or liquid; erythema spreads over the next 24 hours and yellowish blisters appear and can become ulcerated. Thinner skin (neck, axillae, and groin) is more susceptible than thicker skin (soles, palms).

157.heading: PEARLS
157.text: INHALATION exposure: Cough, hemoptysis, dyspnea, and possible pulmonary edema may occur up to 24 hours after inhalation of the gas. Ulceration of airway mucose may occur. Mild pulmonary exposure produces rhinorrhea, sneezing, epistaxis, hoarseness, and cough within 12 to 24 hours of exposure. Severe exposure produces additional symptoms of productive cough and shortness of breath (mild to severe) 2 to 4 hours after exposure.

159.heading: CRITERIA
159.text: • Any patient with suspected exposure to a chemical nerve agent or organophosphate AND • Signs / symptoms of exposure, including: o SLUDGE: Excessive salivation, lacrimation, urination, defecation, gastrointestinal distress, or emesis o DUMBBELS: Diarrhea, urinary, miosis, bronchorrhea, bradycardia, emesis, lacrimation, or salivation.

159.heading: PEARLS
159.text: Each DuoDote Autoinjector contains 2.1 mg of Atropine sulfate and 600 mg of Pralodoxime chloride.

159.heading: PEARLS
159.text: Nerve agents include both common organophosphate/carbamate pesticides and military grade toxins. Examples include: Azinphos-methyl, Malathion, Methyl parathion, Aldicarb, Sevin, Bendiocarb, Sarin, Somen, Tobun, VX, and Novichok.

161.heading: CRITERIA
161.text: • Any patient with confirmed or suspected exposure to harmful radiation.

161.heading: PEARLS
161.text: *Treatment of seriously injured or ill radiologically contaminated patients takes priority over decontamination. Do not delay advanced life support to assess contamination status.

161.heading: PEARLS
161.text: Contaminated patients from a Radiation Dispersal Device present a low risk of exposure to healthcare providers.

161.heading: PEARLS
161.text: Patients with open wounds should have the wound dressed and bandages without cleaning.

161.heading: PEARLS
161.text: Responders should wear a minimum of N-95 respirators when responding to non-specific explosions to reduce the change of internal contamination.

161.heading: PEARLS
161.text: The mother likely isotopes used for Radiation Dispersal Devices will emit Gamma radiation, in addition to Alpha and Beta particles. Therefore, most available detectors will identify contamination. However, the dispersal of a source reduces the level of radioactivity, and therefore detection above background levels may be difficult.

161.heading: PEARLS
161.text: When monitoring for patient contamination (external), use of the portal monitors (found at several hospital emergency departments and available through the Hampton Roads Metropolitan Medical Strike Team) and/or the use of hand-held ratemeters with a “pancake” probe is suggested. When using a hand-held ratemeter, a quick “triage” of contamination should focus on the head (hair) and feet (shoes), with a more extensive survey on those found to be contaminated.

231.heading: INDICATIONS
231.text: • As indicated by any of the following protocols: o Allergic Reaction / Anaphylaxis o Overdose / Poisoning / Toxic Ingestion o Bradycardia (Symptomatic) o Post-Cardiac Arrest Care (ROSC) o Chest Pain (Cardiac) o Seizure o Crush Injuries o Tachyarrhythmias o Hypotension and Shock • Any witnessed or reported syncope, altered mental status, respiratory distress, and/or any condition or presentation which raises suspicion for an acute coronary syndrome, cardiac ischemia, or dysrhythmia.

232.heading: PEARLS
232.text: Dry with a towel or shave the chest as needed if electrodes will not adhere or signal cannot becaptured.

232.heading: PEARLS
232.text: Consider patient privacy, modesty, and cultural preferences. Consider moving out of public view prior to removing clothing.

232.heading: PEARLS
232.text: Signs of ischemia (including S-T elevation) cannot be accurately or adequately assessed via 2- or 4-Lead ECG. A 12-Lead ECG is required to assess for ischemia.

232.heading: PEARLS
232.text: If a 12-Lead ECG has been transmitted and then a patient refusal is being obtained, consider contacting medical control to ensure there are no additional findings which the patient may require to make an informed decision.

232.heading: PEARLS
232.text: The initial ECGs may not show ischemia. When there is high suspicion for cardiac ischemia, obtain serial ECGs (approx. 10 minutes apart) to assess for changes and the development of signs of ischemia.

232.heading: PEARLS
232.text: If possible, obtain a 12-Lead ECG prior to the release of a crush injury followed by serial ECGs once released.

232.heading: PEARLS
232.text: Intermediate and Paramedic providers may interpret a 12-Lead ECG as STEMI if diagnostic criteria ismet: o Symptoms consistent with an acute coronary syndrome or myocardial infarction AND o ≥ 1 mm ST segment elevation in two or more contiguous leads

232.heading: PEARLS
232.text: EMT-I and Paramedic: If there is >1 mm ST elevation in leads II, III, and/or V1, and the ECG reads STEMI/ACUTE MI, consider obtaining a right-sided (V4R) ECG. See diagram below for lead placement. Transmit and consult medical control prior to administering Nitroglycerine. o ST elevation > 1 mm in lead V4R is highly sensitive for right ventricular infarction. o Patients with acute right ventricular infarction are highly preload dependent. Avoid nitrates unless specifically ordered by Medical Control.

232.heading: PEARLS
232.text: A Right-sided 12-Lead ECG (V4R) & Posterior 12-Lead ECG (V8 & V9) together constitute a 15-LeadECG: o V4R- (formerly V4)5th intercostal space at midclavicular line on the patient’s right side o V8 - (formerly V5) 6th intercostal space left posterior at midscapular line o V9 - (formerly V6) 6th intercostal space left at paraspinous line o Label the second 12-Lead ECG to reflect the new leads: V4 as V4R, V5 as V8, and V6 as V9

235.heading: CRITERIA
235.text: • Patient unresponsive, without palpable pulse or respiration (excluding agonal breaths). • Patients with obvious death (rigor mortis, lividity, decomposition, or injuries inconsistent with survival) are excluded.

236.heading: PEARLS
236.text: Push hard and fast: rate 100 – 120 bpm. Allow complete chest recoil.

236.heading: PEARLS
236.text: Change compressor every 2 minutes or sooner iffatigued.

236.heading: PEARLS
236.text: Give continuous compressions with advanced airway.

236.heading: PEARLS
236.text: Use quantitative ETCO2 monitoring with BVM o If ETCO2 < 10 mmHg, improve chestcompressions o If sudden increase in ETCO2 isnoted (above 30-40mmHg), check pulse and rhythm for ROSC.

236.heading: PEARLS
236.text: Avoid excessive ventilation. Consider supraglottic airway (BIAD) or endotracheal intubation. (EMT)

236.heading: PEARLS
236.text: Studies to date have not shown a clear improvement in outcomes with SGA vs intubation – do not compromise chest compressions for intubation.

236.heading: PEARLS
236.text: Use ETCO2 to confirm and monitor placement of anyadvanced airway.

236.heading: PEARLS
236.text: Continually monitor ETCO2 with target above 10 mmHg during CPR and 35 - 45 mmHg if ROSC is achieved.

236.heading: PEARLS
236.text: In post ROSC patient, if ETCO2 falls below 20 mmHg or signal is lost, immediately reassess pulses and airway.

236.heading: PEARLS
236.text: Ensure pad placement is optimal. Adjust pads if shockable rhythm is refractory to electrical therapy. Consider Anterior/Posterior placement.

236.heading: PEARLS
236.text: Use maximum joules setting for adult defibrillation.

236.text: Reversible causes: Identify and treat per appropriate protocol and scope of practice:

236.text: Refer to Death & Criteria for Withholding Resuscitationprotocol.

236.text: Termination of resuscitative efforts is a Medical Control decisiononly.
